posts.title: How Should You Prepare Your Home for a Showing?
posts.excerpt: Staging isn't decorating. It's removing every reason a buyer might hesitate.
posts.metaDescription: How to stage and prepare your home for showings as a FSBO seller: lighting, decluttering, room-by-room preparation, and what buyers notice first.

body.p: If you're going to sell a product, it needs to look good. That's the whole premise of staging, and it applies to a $180,000 starter home as much as it does to anything at the top of your market.
The goal isn't to make your home look like a magazine. It's to make it easy for a stranger to picture their life in it — and to give them nothing to hesitate about.

Family photos, collections, trophies, and the wall of kids' artwork all make a home yours, which is exactly the problem. A buyer walking past your family history is reminded, constantly, that this is someone else's house.
Pack the personal items first. Then clear flat surfaces — counters, the dining table, dressers, the coffee table — leaving three or four intentional pieces where there were twenty.

body.h: Light is the cheapest upgrade you have

body.p: Open every blind and curtain. Turn on every light in the house, including the ones you never use, and replace any bulb that's burnt out or a different color temperature than its neighbors. Wash the windows so the natural light actually gets in.
Dim, closed-up rooms read as small and slightly sad. The same room with light in it reads as bigger. Nothing you can buy delivers that much perceived value for that little money.

Do this before every single showing, not just the first one. It takes about four minutes once you know the route, and buyers touring at four in the afternoon deserve the same house the ten o'clock buyers saw. Sellers get lax about it by the second week, right when the remaining buyers are the most price-sensitive ones.

list: Kitchen — clear the counters to three or four essentials, towels and soaps out of sight, small appliances packed away
Bathrooms — make them look barely used; medications, cosmetics, and styling tools stored out of view
Bedrooms — thin the closets so the space reads as generous, beds made, surfaces clear
Living areas — remotes, magazines, toys, and throws gathered into bins or closets
Garage — the most daunting and most skipped; donate or discard, then shelve what's left

body.pull: You are not tidying. You are removing every question a buyer could ask about the house instead of about their future in it.

body.p: Not fun, but it matters. Pets are wonderful and they are not a selling feature. Dander is a genuine obstacle for allergic buyers, and pet bowls, beds, and litter boxes raise questions about what's been running through the house.
Minimize the evidence, and get pets out of the home during showings if you possibly can.

Walk the route a buyer will walk, in order, and look at what they'll see at each turn. Set the thermostat somewhere comfortable. Take out the trash. Deal with any smell you've grown used to — cooking, pets, damp — because you won't notice it and they will immediately.

Knowing which of these actually affects offers in your price range, versus which are just effort, is the kind of thing our flat-fee guidance at HomePilot helps sellers sort out before the first showing rather than after the third.
Buyers decide fast. Give them a bright, clear, unremarkable-in-the-best-way house, and let them start imagining.

posts.title: Why Should You Care About Your Buyer's Loan Approval?
posts.excerpt: An unqualified buyer doesn't just waste your Saturday. They can cost you weeks of market momentum.
posts.metaDescription: How to qualify buyers as a FSBO seller: pre-approval vs pre-qualification, loan types, and why an unverified buyer can cost you weeks on the market.

body.p: A buyer calls, wants to see the house today, sounds genuinely excited. You ask whether they've spoken to a lender. There's a pause. "A lender? Like, for a loan?"
That conversation happens more than you'd think, and it's the reason to build one habit early: verify before you invest time.

body.h: The real cost of an unqualified buyer

body.p: Showing a house to someone who can't buy it costs you an afternoon. That's annoying but survivable. The expensive version is accepting an offer from someone who can't close.

When that happens, your listing goes off the market, other buyers move on, and thirty days later you're back on with a stale date on your listing and the market's momentum spent. That's the outcome to protect against.

These sound interchangeable and are not. A pre-qualification is generally based on information the buyer told a lender about themselves. A pre-approval means the lender has actually verified income, assets, and credit.

Ask for a pre-approval letter, ideally with a lender's name and phone number on it. Then — this is the step sellers skip — call the lender. A two-minute conversation confirming the letter is current and the buyer is still on track is the highest-value phone call in your entire sale.

body.pull: Ask every serious buyer the same question, at the same point, before scheduling. It isn't rude — it's the job.

list: Have you spoken with a lender, and can you send me the pre-approval letter?
What loan program are you using, and what's the down payment?
Are you contingent on selling another home first?
Has anything changed since the letter was issued?

body.p: Any legitimate buyer expects these questions. Reluctance to answer them is itself the answer.

body.h: Why the loan program matters to you

body.p: Different programs bring different requirements, timelines, and appraisal standards, and some come with closing costs that get framed in negotiation as the seller's responsibility — commonly around 3% of the purchase price. Knowing the program up front tells you what to expect and what to watch for in the offer.
It also tells you something about timeline. A cash buyer and a buyer with a program requiring specific property conditions are not the same deal at the same price.

And a cash offer deserves the same scrutiny, just in a different form. Ask for proof of funds — a recent bank or brokerage statement — rather than taking the word "cash" as its own verification. Cash offers skip the lender and the appraisal, which removes two failure points, but only if the money is actually sitting there.

Stay friendly. Also stay slightly formal. It's genuinely tempting to become friends with an enthusiastic buyer, and that's exactly how sellers end up making verbal promises they get held to later. Keep a professional distance and let the paperwork carry the agreements.

Screening buyers, reading their financing, and spotting the terms that will cost you money later is core to what we do with sellers at HomePilot — broker-level review of every offer, at a flat fee rather than a slice of your equity.
Verify first. Your Saturdays and your market momentum are both worth protecting.

posts.title: How Clean Does Your Home Really Need to Be?
posts.excerpt: Cleaner than you think, and in places you wouldn't expect a buyer to look.
posts.metaDescription: How clean a home needs to be to sell: the deep-cleaning checklist for FSBO sellers, why kitchens and bathrooms matter most, and where buyers actually look.

body.p: Cleanliness is the least interesting advice in real estate and among the most reliable. It works when someone sells a car, and it works when you sell a house, for the same reason: spotless reads as well-maintained, and well-maintained reads as valuable.
The honest answer to how clean is: cleaner than you'd keep it to live in, and specifically clean in the places buyers open.
Doing it in the other order means cleaning around your belongings and doing it twice. Clear the surfaces and pack the nonessentials, and the cleaning gets faster and far more effective.

list: Cobwebs out of every corner, and dust the ceiling fans, light fixtures, and blinds
Wash the walls — necessary before any repainting anyway, so it saves time later
All glass: mirrors, screens, patio doors, tabletops
Polish wood surfaces, wipe down leather furniture
Make every appliance shine, inside and out
Scrub sinks, toilets, tubs, showers, faucets, and countertops until they're genuinely impeccable
Grout and tile free of stains, discoloration, and mildew
Wash the windows, clean the treatments, vacuum, shampoo carpets, mop thoroughly

body.p: With the clutter gone, working room by room from top to bottom is the fastest path through it. If the house is large or your time is short, a professional deep clean is money well spent at this stage.

This is the part sellers underestimate. Buyers open cabinets, pantries, closets, and under the sink, because they're assessing storage. What they find in there is information about how the house has been cared for.

So clean inside the cabinets. Remove pest traps and poison from pantries and closets. And don't use the microwave as a bread box or the oven as cookware storage — buyers find both, and both raise questions.

body.pull: Buyers might forgive an unimpressive kid's bedroom. A questionable kitchen or bathroom can cost you the sale outright.

body.h: Kitchens and bathrooms carry disproportionate weight

body.p: The kitchen is where buyers form their opinion of the entire house. Grime, cooking smells, and trash undo everything else you've done. Clean every cabinet surface and don't skip under the sink.
Bathrooms need to be clean and odor-free, full stop. Americans expect two or three of them and they inspect all of them.

Every home has one — cooking, pets, damp, smoke. You've been nose-blind to yours for years. Ask someone who doesn't live there to tell you honestly, then address the cause rather than covering it. Air fresheners announce that something is being covered.

Don't forget the outside, either. Cobwebs under the eaves, a grimy front door, pollen on the porch furniture, and streaked windows all register before a buyer has stepped inside — and they set the expectation for everything that follows. A hose, a bucket, and an hour handles most of it.

Knowing where preparation genuinely changes offers, and where it's just work, is part of what our flat-fee guidance at HomePilot is for — so your effort goes where a buyer in your price range will actually pay for it.
Spotless equals valuable. It's the cheapest lever you have, and almost nobody pulls it all the way.

posts.title: Which Contract Contingencies Actually Protect You?
posts.excerpt: A purchase agreement without the right contingencies is a promise you may not be able to keep safely.
posts.metaDescription: The contingencies every home seller should have in a purchase and sale agreement: inspection, financing, appraisal, title, and closing date protections.

body.p: The purchase and sale agreement is the document that decides what happens when something goes wrong. Not if — when. Something always comes up, and the contract determines whether it's an inconvenience or a loss.

What follows is the bare minimum worth having in writing. There are many other addendums that may apply to your situation and your state, and this isn't legal advice — it's the list to make sure someone qualified has looked at.

Defines the window the buyer has to inspect and to submit requests, and what happens when they do. Without a clear deadline, the inspection period can effectively stay open, leaving you unable to plan and unable to remarket if the deal sours.

Ties the buyer's obligation to actually obtaining their loan, with a deadline. This is your protection against a buyer sitting on your listing for weeks while a lender works out whether they qualify. A dated financing contingency gives you a defined point at which you know.

Sets out what happens if the appraised value comes in below the purchase price. This matters more than sellers expect: the lender lends against the appraisal, not against your agreed price. The contract should say who covers a gap, or that either party may renegotiate.

Ensures title can be delivered clear and that any liens or clouds are identified and resolved before closing. Old liens, unreleased mortgages, and boundary issues surface here, and it's far better that they surface early.
Be specific about the closing date, when possession transfers, and what happens if either side needs to move it. "Around the end of the month" is how disputes start.

Most states require sellers to disclose known material defects in writing, and the requirements vary considerably by state. This isn't a contingency so much as an obligation, and getting it wrong is one of the few selling mistakes that can follow you after closing. Disclose what you know, in writing, and confirm what your state specifically requires.

body.pull: Every contingency has a date attached. Those dates are the real structure of your sale — put them on a calendar the day the offer is signed.

body.h: Two practical protections beyond the contingencies

list: Have the buyer send earnest money to the title company, which holds it at no cost and disburses it at closing. Never hold a buyer's deposit personally.
Do not promise repairs verbally. We've watched a seller's casual offer to handle the furnace "if it goes out" turn into a $6,000 concession during the final walkthrough.

body.h: Read the offer, not your memory of it

body.p: When an offer arrives, read every line as though you've never discussed it. Sellers regularly find they've agreed to cover a share of the buyer's closing costs — often around 3% of the purchase price — because it was framed as routine during negotiation. Catching it before you sign is a conversation. Catching it later is money.

This is precisely where a licensed broker earns their keep for a for-sale-by-owner seller. At HomePilot, contract review and contingency strategy are part of the flat fee, because the terms of your deal deserve the same scrutiny as the price of it.
Get the contingencies right and most problems become manageable. Skip them and one bad surprise becomes your problem alone.

posts.title: Do Your Listing Photos Actually Sell Your Home?
posts.excerpt: The first photo decides whether anyone sees the other nineteen. It's the highest-leverage dollar in your sale.
posts.metaDescription: Why listing photography matters most when selling a home: what to shoot, in what order, and why professional photos return more than any other marketing spend.

body.p: Buyers find homes by scrolling. That means your listing competes as a thumbnail first and a house second, and the thumbnail either earns a click or it doesn't.
Which makes photography the highest-leverage money in a for-sale-by-owner sale. Not the most exciting. The highest-leverage.

Real estate photographers generally charge a few hundred dollars, they own wide lenses and know how to handle interior light, and the difference between their work and a phone in a dim living room is not subtle.
If you're saving thousands by selling without a full-commission agent, this is the obvious place to reinvest a small fraction of it.
Photography magnifies whatever is already there, including clutter. Do the decluttering, cleaning, and light work first — every surface cleared, every bulb working and matched, every blind open.
Photographers won't tidy for you, and a shoot of an unprepared house produces expensive pictures of clutter.

list: The strongest exterior, in good light — usually morning or late afternoon, never harsh midday
Kitchen, from the angle that shows the most counter and the most depth
The main living space
Primary bedroom, then remaining bedrooms
Bathrooms, clean and depersonalized
Backyard, outdoor spaces, and any genuine feature — a view, a shop, a finished basement

body.p: Lead with whichever of the first three is genuinely your best. If your kitchen is the strongest thing about the house, that's your first photo, not the front elevation.

body.pull: Twenty good photos beat forty mediocre ones. Every weak photo invites a buyer to stop scrolling for the wrong reason.

body.p: Don't photograph the laundry closet, the garage full of boxes, or the unfinished corner of the basement. You're not hiding anything — those things will be seen at the showing — but a listing gallery is a highlight reel, and a weak frame does active damage.
Avoid heavy editing too. Skies dropped in and rooms brightened past reality set up a buyer to be disappointed in person, and disappointment at a showing costs more than a plain photo ever would.

A simple floor plan is one of the most requested and least common additions to a listing. Photos show buyers what rooms look like; a floor plan shows them how the house works — where the bedrooms sit relative to each other, whether the kitchen opens to the living space. Most photographers will add one for a modest fee, and it answers the questions buyers otherwise have to schedule a showing to resolve.

body.h: Then write the first two lines

body.p: Most buyers read the opening of the description and nothing more. Lead with specifics — new roof, updated kitchen, lot size, school — rather than adjectives. "Charming" is invisible. "Vinyl plank flooring and a new roof in 2025" gets read.

Getting the presentation right before you go live matters because the first two weeks generate the most traffic your listing will ever see. Making that window count, rather than learning from it, is a lot of what our flat-fee guidance at HomePilot is for.
Spend the few hundred dollars. It's the cheapest thousand dollars you'll ever make.

posts.title: What Happens If the Appraisal Comes In Low?
posts.excerpt: The lender lends against the appraisal, not against your agreed price. Here are your options when they disagree.
posts.metaDescription: What to do when a home appraisal comes in below the purchase price: appraisal gaps, renegotiation options, and how sellers can prepare for the appraiser.

body.p: An appraisal is a value judgment on your property, performed by a licensed appraiser acting as an unbiased third party. That value goes to whoever is lending your buyer money.

Which is the whole reason it can end your sale. The lender doesn't lend against the price you and the buyer agreed on. It lends against the appraised value. If those two numbers don't match, somebody has to cover the difference.

Say you're under contract at $310,000 and the appraisal comes back at $295,000. The lender will finance based on $295,000, leaving a $15,000 gap. From there the possibilities are limited and fairly clear:

list: The buyer covers the gap in cash, if they have it and want the house enough
You reduce the price, in whole or in part
You split the difference and both move
You dispute the appraisal with supporting comparable sales
The deal terminates under the appraisal contingency

body.p: Which of those is available to you depends on what your purchase agreement says — which is why the appraisal contingency deserves attention before you're in this situation rather than during it.

body.h: How to reduce the odds up front

body.p: Most low appraisals trace back to a list price the comparable sales didn't support. Pricing from three or four genuinely comparable closed sales in the last ninety days, adjusted honestly for condition, is the best protection there is. If your price only makes sense with an optimistic adjustment, an appraiser is unlikely to agree with you.

body.pull: An appraiser can only credit improvements they know about. Handing them a list is not lobbying — it's supplying data.

body.h: Help the appraiser do their job

body.p: You can't influence the outcome, and you shouldn't try. You can supply information. Have ready:

list: A written list of updates with dates and costs — roof, HVAC, flooring, kitchen, windows
Permits and receipts for significant work
Comparable sales you relied on, especially recent ones an out-of-area appraiser might miss
Anything not visible from a walkthrough: a new sewer line, upgraded electrical, insulation

body.p: A new $10,000 roof can add roughly its cost to your value — but only if the appraiser knows it's there. Make sure they do.

Present the house for the appraisal the way you would for a showing, too. Appraisers are professionals valuing condition, not buyers being charmed, but condition is genuinely part of their assessment — and a clean, well-lit, accessible home is easier to appraise favorably than one where the crawlspace is blocked and half the lights are out.

body.h: If it comes in low anyway

body.p: Don't react in the first hour. Read the report and check the comparables it used; appraisers occasionally use sales that aren't genuinely comparable, and a dispute supported by better data sometimes succeeds. Then look at your own position honestly — your timeline, your next purchase, what a relist would cost you in time and momentum.

This is a moment where having someone who has seen the outcome dozens of times matters more than at almost any other point in the transaction. Working through appraisal gaps and renegotiation is part of the flat fee at HomePilot, because the decision is worth more than the paperwork.
Price it where the data supports, document your improvements, and the appraisal is usually a formality rather than a crisis.

posts.title: Should You Accept the First Offer You Get?
posts.excerpt: An early offer feels like proof more is coming. Sometimes it is. Often it's the best one you'll see.
posts.metaDescription: Should home sellers accept the first offer? How to evaluate an early offer, when to wait for a bidding war, and the risk of banking on more buyers.

body.p: An offer lands on day two. Suddenly you're certain the house will sell easily, and maybe a bidding war is coming. Why accept the first thing that arrives?
Maybe you shouldn't. But this is one of the most expensive places for confidence to go unexamined, so it's worth thinking through carefully rather than instinctively.

body.h: Why an early offer is often a good offer

body.p: The buyers who move fastest are usually the ones who have been looking longest. They know the inventory, they recognize a home that fits when they see it, and they're pre-approved and ready because they've already lost out on something.
So the question to sit with is this: if a buyer wants your home badly enough to make a solid offer on the first day, do you really want to set them aside and hope for people who are less interested?

body.h: The math of the first two weeks

body.p: Your listing generates the most traffic it will ever see in its first two weeks, because everyone with a matching saved search gets notified the day you go live. That's your peak audience, not a preview of a rising one.

After that, weekly traffic declines and your listing accumulates days on market — which buyers read as a signal that something's wrong. Banking on a bidding war can cost you a quick, clean sale and leave you negotiating from a weaker position a month later.

body.pull: Let every showing that's already booked go ahead before you decide. It's fair to the people who scheduled, and it creates real competition rather than hypothetical competition.

body.h: A rule of thumb that works

body.p: Don't accept or reject on the spot. Let the showings already on the calendar proceed as scheduled, then decide.

This is a practice buyers respect — you're honoring people who booked before them — and it lets you mention, professionally and accurately, that there's an offer in hand to the people already serious enough to be touring. That's how genuine competition gets created, and it's very different from turning down a good offer to wait for a better one that may not exist.

body.h: Read the terms, not just the number

list: Is the buyer pre-approved, and have you called the lender to confirm?
How much earnest money, and is it going to the title company?
What closing costs are you being asked to cover? Some loan programs push roughly 3% of the price onto the seller.
Is the offer contingent on selling another home?
Does the closing date work for your own move?

body.p: A slightly lower price with clean terms and a verified buyer frequently nets you more than a higher price attached to conditions and uncertainty.

You're weighing a real offer in hand against a hypothetical better one. Evaluating that honestly — against your market's inventory, your timeline, and the actual terms in front of you — is exactly the kind of call we help sellers make at HomePilot, on a flat fee rather than a commission that grows with your price.
A strong early offer is usually a signal you priced it right, not a sign you priced it too low.

posts.title: What Do You Do If Your Sale Falls Through?
posts.excerpt: Deals collapse for ordinary reasons. What you do in the next 48 hours determines what it costs you.
posts.metaDescription: What to do when a home sale falls through: earnest money, relisting strategy, days on market, and how sellers should respond to a failed transaction.

body.p: The financing fell apart. The inspection scared them off. They found something else. Whatever the cause, you're back where you started with time on the clock and a listing that now has history.
It's a bad day. It's also common, recoverable, and largely a question of how quickly and deliberately you respond.

Don't let earnest money go without reviewing the buyer's contractual position first. Whether they're entitled to a refund depends on which contingency they terminated under and whether they met the deadlines in the agreement.

If they exited properly within an active contingency, the money generally goes back. If they walked outside those terms, you may have a claim to some or all of it. Read the agreement before you agree to anything, and get qualified help if the amount is meaningful.
This matters more than the disappointment, because the reason determines your next move:

list: Financing failed — often nothing to do with your house; verify the next buyer's pre-approval more carefully
Inspection findings — you now know what the next inspector will find, which is genuinely useful information
Low appraisal — a signal your price may be ahead of what comparable sales support
Cold feet — no lesson, just bad luck

body.p: Only two of those suggest changing anything about your listing. Don't cut your price over a buyer's lending problem.

body.h: Fix what you learned before relisting

body.p: If the inspection surfaced real defects, address them or price them in. The next buyer's inspector will find the same things, and you'll be having the same conversation from a weaker position — now with a failed sale in your listing history.
You may also have disclosure obligations regarding what the inspection revealed, depending on your state. That's worth confirming rather than assuming.

body.pull: Move quickly. Days on market accumulate whether or not you were under contract, and buyers read that number.

body.h: Get back on the market fast

body.p: Momentum matters. Every week off the market with a stale date attached makes the listing look more troubled than it is. Refresh the photos if anything has changed, consider a genuinely revised description, and get back in front of the saved-search audience.
Some of the buyers who toured during your first two weeks are still looking. It's entirely reasonable to let serious previous prospects know the home is available again.

body.h: And be a little more careful this time

body.p: Verify pre-approval and call the lender. Keep earnest money with the title company. Put every contract deadline on a calendar the day the next offer is signed. Most failed sales trace back to something that could have been caught earlier.

Recovering from a broken deal — sorting the earnest money question, deciding what to fix, and getting relisted without losing your position — is exactly the kind of stretch where broker-level guidance earns its cost. At HomePilot that's part of the flat fee, not a new negotiation.
One collapsed deal is a setback, not a verdict on your house. Handle the next 48 hours well and it usually stays a setback.

posts.title: Are Your Pets Costing You Money on Your Sale?
posts.excerpt: Nobody enjoys this conversation. It's still one of the most common avoidable discounts we see.
posts.metaDescription: How pets affect home sale price: odor, dander, damage, and what pet owners should do before showings to avoid lower offers from buyers.

body.p: Let's be upfront: this isn't a fun subject, and it isn't a judgment about your animals. It's a practical point about what buyers notice, and it costs sellers real money often enough to be worth saying plainly.
Pets are wonderful. They are not a feature of your home, and buyers want to see the house without them.
It helps to split this up, because the fixes are different.

list: Odor. The biggest one, and the one you genuinely cannot assess yourself — you've been nose-blind to your own home for years.
Dander and allergies. A meaningful share of buyers are allergic, and a reaction during a showing ends the showing emotionally, whatever they say politely.
Visible evidence. Bowls, beds, crates, litter boxes, scratched trim, worn carpet paths. Each one raises the question of what has been running through this house.

body.p: Ask a friend who hasn't been to your home recently to walk in and tell you the truth. Not "does it smell bad" — ask "what do you smell?" You need a real answer, and most people will soften it unless you ask for the unsoftened version.

Then treat the cause rather than covering it. Carpet and padding hold odor at the padding level, so surface cleaning often isn't enough; professional treatment or replacement is sometimes the only real fix. Hard floors need the grout and baseboards addressed. Air fresheners and plug-ins broadcast that something is being masked, which is worse than a faint smell.

body.pull: Buyers assign far more value to negatives than positives. A pet odor becomes a number in their head before they've seen the second bedroom.

body.p: Get the animals out of the house if you can — a walk, a neighbor, a few hours at daycare. Barring that, they should be genuinely out of the way rather than in a crate in the middle of the living room.

Then remove the evidence: bowls and mats put away, beds and toys in a closet, litter box cleaned and stored, throws with hair on them laundered. Vacuum right before, including furniture and the edges of rooms where hair collects.

Scratched door frames, chewed trim, worn carpet in traffic paths, and screen damage all read as deferred maintenance and get valued generously against you. These are inexpensive repairs relative to the discount they invite — the same principle as any other value red flag.
None of this means pet owners can't sell well. It means the presence of pets needs to be minimized rather than explained, so buyers can view the home unimpeded by questions about it.

Knowing which of these actually affects offers in your market — and which are worth the money to fix before listing — is the kind of specific, unsentimental read our flat-fee guidance at HomePilot is built to give sellers.
Take the dog for a long walk on showing day. It's the easiest money in this whole article.

posts.title: Which Small Details Do Sellers Forget Until It's Too Late?
posts.excerpt: The last few items on the list are boring, easy, and genuinely painful to fix after the fact.
posts.metaDescription: The details home sellers forget before closing: canceling utilities, earnest money handling, keys and warranties, and final walkthrough preparation.

body.p: Most of selling a home is strategy — price, presentation, negotiation. Then there's a short list of purely administrative items that nobody thinks about until they've become a problem.
None of these will cost you the sale. Several will cost you money, time, or an unpleasant week after you've already moved.

body.h: Cancel the utilities. Put it on the calendar.

body.p: This is the one sellers forget most, and untangling it later is a genuine pain. Put a calendar reminder tied to your closing date and work through the full list:

list: Water and sewer
Electricity and gas
Trash collection
HOA fees and dues
Irrigation
Internet, security monitoring, and anything else on autopay

body.p: Time the cancellations for the day after closing, not before. A house with the water off during a final walkthrough creates problems, and a buyer can't verify that plumbing works without it.

body.h: Never hold the earnest money yourself

body.p: Ask the buyer to send earnest money to the title company, which holds it at no cost and disburses it appropriately at closing. Holding a buyer's deposit personally is a lawsuit waiting to happen, and it gains you nothing whatsoever.

Worth repeating because it keeps happening. A seller who was friendly with his buyers casually said they'd handle the air conditioning "if it happens to go out." The furnace died during the final walkthrough. The buyers refused to sign, and he paid $6,000 to close a sale he'd already moved out for.
Stay friendly and stay slightly formal. Let the buyer raise their own concerns, then make a judgment call once you know what they actually care about.

body.pull: Prorated taxes, HOA dues, and utilities are settled at closing. Your share is real money — know it before you see the settlement statement.

body.h: Gather the paperwork buyers will want

list: Appliance manuals and any transferable warranties
Receipts and permits for major work — roof, HVAC, electrical, windows
Paint colors and any remaining matched paint
HOA documents, rules, and contact information
Every key, garage remote, mailbox key, gate code, and alarm code

body.p: Assembling this in a single folder takes an hour and makes the closing table dramatically less stressful. Missing keys and unrecorded gate codes are a surprisingly common last-minute scramble.

The buyer will walk the home shortly before closing, expecting it broom-clean, empty of everything not included in the sale, and in the condition it was in when they agreed to buy it. Leave nothing behind that wasn't negotiated — including the items in the garage you were hoping they wouldn't mind.

body.h: Then run your net proceeds one more time

body.p: Sale price, minus your loan payoff, minus professional fees, minus prorated expenses, minus any costs you agreed to cover. Knowing that number before you sit down means no unpleasant math at the table.

Catching the small items before they become expensive ones is unglamorous and it's most of what a good advisor actually does. At HomePilot it's part of the flat fee — the checklist work included, not billed by the hour.
Boring, quick, and much easier now than in three weeks.
